query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In multilayer high‐entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings, the engineered interfaces act as barriers that block and slow dislocation motion and climb, thereby reducing creep (time‐dependent plastic deformation) relative to a similar monolithic HEA coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer protective coating comprised of HEA layers produced by a controlled deposition process (e.g., magnetron sputtering or laser cladding) that yields well‐defined alternating layers with high lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Introduce and control the multilayer architecture by engineering deposition parameters (such as bias voltage or layer thickness) so that coatings have distinct, coherent interfaces, and compare these with a monolithic (single-layer) HEA coating made under the same overall processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Creep tests (e.g., nanoindentation creep) performed under elevated temperature and constant load conditions matching service regimes. The interface-rich coatings and monolithic control are both evaluated under identical temperature, stress, and environmental settings.
generation.structural_mediator: The well‐defined multilayer interfaces, which due to lattice mismatch and high intrinsic distortion, act as barriers to dislocation motion and prevent dislocation climb.
generation.mechanism: Under applied stress and high temperature, dislocations in the HEA layers are generated. In multilayer coatings, the interfaces obstruct dislocation glide and climb, increasing the effective activation energy for creep by forcing dislocations to pile up or change paths. This resistance mechanism is less effective in a monolithic HEA coating where dislocations move more freely.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the monolithic HEA coating (baseline), the multilayer coating will exhibit a lower creep strain (or reduced creep rate) under identical testing conditions, reflecting enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous, monolithic high-entropy alloy coating produced under the same overall processing conditions but lacking engineered, periodic interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be most effective at operational temperatures and stresses where dislocation-mediated creep is dominant and where diffusion is sufficiently slow (typical for HEAs), and it may be less significant if testing conditions fall outside the high-temperature regime or if layer thicknesses are not in the optimal range for interface effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: While the hypothesis attributes the creep resistance mainly to interface-induced dislocation blockage, the exact quantitative contributions of lattice distortion and slow diffusion inherent to HEAs remain to be fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one set with an engineered multilayer architecture (with controlled, high-quality interfaces) and a control set as a monolithic HEA coating, ensuring both are processed under identical overall conditions. Subject both sets to nanoindentation creep tests at the same elevated temperature and constant load. Use post-test microscopy to examine dislocation distributions near the interfaces.
measurements: Time-dependent creep strain (or creep rate) under constant load
Activation energy for creep (extracted from temperature-dependent tests)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM) identifying dislocation pile-ups or blockage at interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain (or creep rate) compared to the monolithic control, or if microstructural analysis reveals no evidence of dislocation blocking or pile-up at interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Each temperature-dependent curve in the plot can be divided into two distinct regions. Each temperature-dependent curve can be divided into two distinct stress regimes. In the low-stress regime, the extracted stress exponents fall within the diffusion-controlled range defined by Equation (4), whereas at higher stresses, the stress exponent increases markedly, indicating a transition to dislocation-dominated creep. These findings are consistent with atomic-scale observations and corroborate the proposed creep mechanism transitions. Similarly, Figure 9b shows the stress exponent n for HEA, ranging from 1.08 to 11.37. A similar stress-dependent behavior is observed for HEA, with stress exponents evolving from the diffusion-dominated regime at low stresses to dislocation-controlled deformation at higher stresses, following the same mechanistic framework as HESA. Therefore, stress-dependent creep mechanisms in HEA are essentially analogous to those observed in HESA. In service, one of the essential design criteria for engineering components is the time-dependent deformation behavior (i.e., creep resistance). Macroscopic bulk compression or tension [,,], micro-pillar compression [,], and nano-indentation technique [,,,,,,] have been used to investigate the deformation behavior of materials in a wide range of length scales. Major discrepancies between the data obtained by nano-indentation and via conventional creep testing (i.e., compression/tension) have been reported [,]. This may be due to the complex multi-axial and inhomogeneous stress below indenters in comparison with uniaxial and homogeneous stress during bulk compression/tension test []. Despite these discrepancies, nano-indentation has been used as a convenient and fast approach to characterize the time-dependent deformation behavior at the small-scale for pure metals [,], bulk metallic glasses [,], and HEAs [,,,,,,,]. Most nano-indentation creep studies are limited to room temperature, low load (<100 mN), and face-centered cubic (FCC) metals/alloys [,,,,,,].
